I would recommend this app for anybody that’s had a visit with a doctor, and hasn’t recalled all of the responses. In a short period of time, Kin produced concise summary of a visit with my specialist. It’s so simple: set up the free app; bring your phone to a visit; tell the doctor you’d like to record; press start, and then stop. In a short time you get a report for your use, or share with a family member.

In addition to personal visits, you can record a telephone conversation. There’s an extra step because you can’t speak and record on the same device. You can take a call over your Mac or PC, and use your phone to record. This is a great app, and I’d recommend highly.

title.label: Genuinely impressed by the utility of this app

content.label:
I was initially skeptical, but this app has proven to be incredibly useful. Managing my care across a new network of providers (including surgical, HRT, general wellness, physical therapy and psychiatry) can be overwhelming. This app helps me manage referrals and checklists by discreetly recording and transcribing each appointment. It documents every detail and provides an accurate, actionable to-do list with all of the relevant information easily accessible after each visit. It functions flawlessly for in-person calls, tele-health appointments, specialist referrals and even cosmetic/plastic surgery consultations.

I'm so grateful to the entire team behind Kin and genuinely enthusiastic about what's ahead.

That said, there are a few little problems with the app that I'm sure the developer can easily work out. For example, if you set it up with your calendar and an appointment is scheduled but you change the date of the appointment, the app fails to recognize this. It keeps the original date and does not add the new date, which may confuse you when you're suddenly told in the morning that you have an appointment that day, but you really don't. Otherwise, it does everything that it's supposed to do

1 STAR — Misleading about control of your data

Be VERY CAUTIOUS!  Once they create the visit summary it could become a permanent part of your medical record and if it’s inaccurate, too bad, you’re stuck with it!!

Kin states on its website: “You own your data” and “Your data is private by default and always in your control.”

I relied on those statements when using Kin to record an important conversation on my own phone. I later discovered that I cannot access the original audio recording.

I find it very difficult to reconcile “You own your data” and “always in your control” with being unable to obtain your own recording.

If Kin does not provide users access to the original audio, that should be made unmistakably clear before they record, not after.

Be very careful using Kin for anything where the original recording might matter.

Attempts to appeal their decision falls on deaf ears.

This app may collect audio recordings and transcripts of private medical appointments, and those conversations may be processed by third-party API providers. Before pressing record, users should know exactly where their doctor-patient conversation goes, what is retained, what is deleted, and how this free, venture-backed app plans to make money.

Kin’s privacy materials raise serious questions. Does Kin delete the original audio after transcription? How long are transcripts, summaries, and backups retained? What exact data does Kin keep after each visit? Can Kin use deidentified or aggregated medical conversation data to improve products, analytics, or future models? Can that data ever be shared, transferred, licensed, sold, or used commercially? What happens to user data if Kin is acquired?

Saying third-party providers are restricted from training general-purpose AI models on user data does not answer these core questions. Doctor visits can include diagnoses, prescriptions, mental health, reproductive health, family history, insurance issues, and other deeply personal information.

The privacy disclosure should be impossible to miss before recording begins: whether the audio leaves the phone, whether outside API providers process it, what is stored, what is deleted, how long data is retained, and what rights Kin claims over deidentified or aggregated health data.

Until those answers are clear, users should be very cautious about recording doctor visits with Kin.
